prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. My case does not rest on nostalgia or on a claim that cursive makes children cleverer. It rests on three plainer points. Writing by hand remains a daily tool for most children for at least the next decade. A joined hand is usually faster and easier to sustain than printed letters once it is learned. The cost of teaching it is small enough that dropping it would save very little.

Start with what the curriculum asks. In England the national curriculum for key stage 1 and key stage 2 sets out a gradual path. In Year 2, children are expected to begin using the diagonal and horizontal strokes that join letters. In Years 3 and 4 they are expected to use those strokes and to judge which neighbouring letters are better left unjoined. That is a modest requirement. It does not call for copperplate or for hours of drill. A teacher can cover it in short sessions of ten or fifteen minutes, a few times a week, over about three years. The proposal to drop it is a proposal to save those minutes, and the question is what they would otherwise be spent on.

The usual answer is keyboards. Children will type for most of their working lives, the argument goes, so time on pen control is time taken from the skill they will use. I accept the premise about adulthood and reject the conclusion for primary school. Children aged five to eleven still do most of their schoolwork by hand. They write answers in exercise books, copy from the board, take part in spelling tests and sit written exams. Few primary schools have enough devices for each child to type every day, and fewer still would want that. Until typing is the main way children produce work in the classroom, handwriting is the main way, and a skill that is used every school day deserves proper teaching.

The research on handwriting and learning is often overstated by supporters of cursive, so I will describe it with care. A well-known 2014 study by Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer compared students who took lecture notes by hand with those who typed them. The typists wrote more words, but the handwriters did better on conceptual questions afterwards. The researchers' explanation was that typists tend to transcribe the lecture almost word for word, while handwriters, who cannot keep up, have to summarise. Later attempts to repeat the result have had mixed outcomes, so I treat it as suggestive and not settled. It also involved university students and said nothing about joined writing specifically.

The evidence on young children is closer to the point. Karin James and her colleagues at Indiana University scanned the brains of children who had not yet learned to read. After the children practised letters by hand, regions used in reading became more active than after they practised by typing or tracing. A Norwegian team led by Audrey van der Meer recorded brain activity in students as they wrote words by hand and by keyboard, and found richer connectivity patterns during handwriting. These studies are small, and none of them compares joined with printed writing. What they support is that forming letters with a pen engages the child differently from pressing keys. That is a reason to keep teaching handwriting. It does not on its own show that joining the letters adds anything.

For the joining itself, the argument is practical. Printed letters require the pen to leave the page after every stroke or every letter. A joined hand lets the pen move through a whole word, which cuts the number of lifts and restarts. Teachers who use it report that it helps with spelling, because the hand learns common letter strings as single movements. That is a view held by many classroom teachers, and I find it plausible, but I would not call it proven. Where the evidence is firmer is on fluency in general. Steve Graham and other researchers at Arizona State University have reviewed many studies of handwriting instruction and found that teaching it improves the speed and quality of children's writing. Berninger's work at the University of Washington found that children in the primary grades wrote longer and more complete compositions by hand than at a keyboard. When transcription costs a child less effort, more attention is left for the content of the sentence. A child who must think about every letter shape writes shorter pieces and loses the thread of what they meant to say.

Speed matters most at the point where it affects a grade. In timed written exams, a child whose hand is slow or tiring will write less than they know. The children who benefit most from a fluent hand are not the ones who find school easy. They are the ones who already struggle to get ideas onto paper, and for them any gain in speed lowers the barrier to showing what they understand. I hold the view that a fluent, joined hand is among the cheapest ways to help such children, because it needs only a pen and some structured practice.

The strongest objection is that there is no clear proof that joined writing beats a well-formed print hand. I agree that the evidence is thin. Some studies suggest that fast, legible writers can be found in both groups, and some fast writers use a mix of joined and unjoined letters, as the English curriculum itself anticipates. The sensible response is to teach a joined style as the default and to allow children to settle on a personal hand, as most adults do. A good print hand is better than a poor cursive one. But the lack of a decisive comparison cuts both ways. Nobody has shown that dropping joined writing improves anything, and the risk of dropping it falls on children who would have gained from it.

There are also arguments from access. Cursive is how a large share of handwritten documents from the last few centuries were written, including wills, letters, parish registers and census returns. A child who cannot read joined writing is cut off from much of this material without help. Many adults also sign their names in a joined hand, and a signature is still how many legal and financial documents are validated. These are modest points and I do not rest the case on them, but they add weight to a position already supported on other grounds. Several American states that had removed cursive from their standards have restored it in recent years. California, for example, passed a law in 2023 requiring it to be taught in the early grades. That change came partly from parents and teachers who noticed that children could not read their grandparents' handwriting or sign their own names with confidence.

A further point concerns children with dysgraphia and other motor difficulties. It is sometimes argued that joined writing is harder for them and that printing or typing should replace it. Occupational therapists differ on this. Some find that the continuous movement of a joined hand suits children who have trouble deciding where each letter starts, and others find that it adds difficulty. The right response is to teach the whole class a joined hand and to give individual help or alternatives, including keyboards, to the children who need them. It would be a mistake to take away a tool from every pupil because it does not suit a minority, as long as the minority is not left without support.

The cost side should be stated plainly. Handwriting lessons use time that could go to reading, number work or science, and primary timetables are full. I think the objection is fair, and the answer is that the time involved is small and the skill pays back across every subject that follows. A child who writes quickly and legibly spends less effort on the mechanics of each sentence in history, science and English for the rest of their schooling. If a few minutes a day for three years produce that, the trade is a good one. I would also ask for those minutes to be taught properly, with correct posture, pencil grip and letter formation, and not left to worksheets of copied lines.

None of this requires schools to ignore keyboards. Children should learn to type, and the sooner they can touch-type with reasonable accuracy the better, probably from around the age of nine or ten. The two skills do different jobs. Typing suits long drafts, editing and work that will be shared or stored. Handwriting suits notes, short answers, exams, labels, cards and anything done away from a screen. A school that teaches both is preparing children for the way people actually write.

My position, then, is a limited one. Joined-up handwriting is not a magic route to better thinking, and its supporters have sometimes claimed too much. But it is a practical skill with a low cost, a reasonable body of evidence behind handwriting instruction as a whole, and a plausible benefit for fluency in the children who need help most. Schools should keep teaching it, teach it well and for a short time each week, and let children adapt it into a hand of their own.
